Nice to meet you

About me

I'm a UX/UI researcher and designer based in New York City. I have a BFA in Fine Arts from Parsons School of Design, an M.S. in Media Management from Parsons and an M.S. in Information Experience Design from Pratt.

I love understanding people: how they think, what motivates them and what frustrates them. My art background gave me an eye for composition, color and storytelling. Research taught me to ask why something works, who it serves and what problem it actually solves.

    Case study · Web · usability research

    The Huntington: Collections Usability Study

    The Huntington's new collections portal was built for scholars and opened to everyone. Our usability study changed course halfway through, and we learned the most once we stopped testing the wrong thing.

    Role
    UX researcher. I moderated 6 of 12 sessions, rewrote our round-two task script and did much of the synthesis.
    Team
    Manvita Kona, Victoria Kagan and me
    Timeline
    October 26 – December 10, 2026
    Method
    Remote, moderated think-aloud usability testing in two rounds
    12participants in two rounds
    9 of 12had no real archive experience
    35round-one issues scored and ranked

    01 · The problem

    A portal built for scholars, opened to everyone

    The Huntington is a research library, art museum and botanical garden that each kept its own online catalog. The beta "Discover Our Collections" portal puts them behind one search box for the first time.

    The client wanted it to work for curious non-experts, but the portal had been built around scholars, and they had no research on general visitors. Most of their traffic goes to the homepage, Plan Your Visit and the events calendar. Could those visitors find the collections, and use them once they did?

    02 · Recruiting

    We recruited for newcomers, not experts

    The client needed to know whether the portal served both scholars and general visitors, so we recruited both. Within each group we wanted a wide range of people, but mostly people with little or no archive experience, so we'd see what a newcomer runs into rather than what an expert knows to work around. One participant was blind and used a screen reader.

    The class required us to recruit through Private Panels. We invited 585 people, 43 answered our screener, and we scheduled eight for 45-minute Zoom sessions with a $10 incentive.

    The screener asked people to rate their archive experience, then explain the rating in their own words. The explanation turned out to matter more. Several people rated themselves moderate or even extensive, but their explanations described little real experience. One picked "Extensive," then wrote that she had limited experience with museum archives. We went by what people described, not the rating.

    For our second round, short on time, we skipped the panel and recruited four more people in person, which was much faster. None had archive experience. Across both rounds, 9 of our 12 participants had no real archive experience.

    03 · Round one

    We started by testing one famous object

    For round one we built every task around the Gutenberg Bible, the collection's most famous object. Its clear right answers (when it was made, how The Huntington got it, whether it's on display) let us compare everyone on the same tasks. Scholars and general visitors each got their own script.

    The results were rough. Nobody found out how The Huntington acquired the Bible, and no one could fully say whether they could see it in person. For someone deciding whether to visit, that's the answer that matters most.

    Round one results, 8 participants
    TaskOn their ownPartly or with helpCouldn't, or got it wrong
    Find the online collections350
    Find the Gutenberg Bible431
    Find out if you can see it in person015 (2 ran out of time)

    In my second session, a participant asked when the Bible was made and read the first date on the record: 1397. That's Gutenberg's birth year. The record opens with his lifespan and never labels the book's own date, around 1455. Unlabeled fields don't just confuse people. They lead to confidently wrong answers.

    The screen reader user never reached the record.

    Nothing on that page signifies that this is the copy… you're looking for.

    Round-one participant

    04 · Changing course

    Then the client told us we'd asked the wrong question

    When we shared early findings, the client told us the tasks missed what they needed to know. Those questions had been in our kickoff notes all along. Do people search or filter? Do they notice the links to the library catalog and the Art Museum's separate catalog? Do they use the garden maps, understand the record fields, move between collections, or use the curator-built "Collection Connections" themes?

    We'd drifted toward a known-item search because it was easy to score. It just wasn't the test this client needed.

    1. Browse with no goal

      Four new participants started on the homepage and explored freely.

    2. Find a landscape painting

      From the Art Museum's collection.

    3. Find a plant using the collections search

      From the Botanical Gardens.

    4. Find historical plant illustrations

      Works best if you combine filters across collections, so it tested whether people understood the portal spans all three.

    So I rewrote the script around browsing, and follow-up questions went straight at the client's list. I also started logging, from each recording, what people did without saying it. Some of the study's best evidence came from that log.

    05 · Round two findings

    What people did when they were free to browse

    Given no goal, people skipped the search bar

    The landing page puts a big search box above the Collection Connections themes: Pets, Tea, Roses, Women Artists and more. Every round-two participant scrolled past the search to the themes. Two went straight into one, and a third said she'd pick them over search "because I'm more visual."

    The name didn't stick, though. One participant browsed the Tea theme early on, then later said he'd never seen anything called Collection Connections. For newcomers, browsing is the real front door, but the feature needs a name and placement that stick.

    The answer to our hardest task was already on the page

    One participant never finished the illustration task. The others got there by trial and error, past results like photos of industrial pumping plants. Meanwhile, curators had already built a "Botanical Illustrations" theme with exactly what the task asked for. Nobody opened it during the task, and three participants scrolled right past it at other times. The curators' best work stays hidden unless themes show up where people are already searching.

    Records raised more questions than they answered

    Three of four round-two participants couldn't tell what "Date" meant on a plant record: when it was planted, photographed or acquired. Terms like "accession number" meant nothing to them. On-view status only appeared on the Art Museum's separate catalog: "I had to click learn more to find out whether or not it was on view; the main site didn't say that." From the record alone, a visitor could plan a trip to see something that isn't on display.

    The best-loved feature was the "Where will I find it?" garden map, "exactly what I would want," one participant said. But it sits below the fold, and some plant records don't have one. It shows what every record could do: tell people where to find the object.

    • The recordings caught what people didn't say

      One participant's Botanical Gardens filter quietly unticked itself twice, and she only noticed once. For two participants, the "Search" breadcrumb wiped their search and filters, dropping them into all 1,029,983 records. And no one I logged ever closed the beta banner warning that records might be incomplete. Problems like these fail silently, so interviews alone would have missed them.

    • Scholars got stuck in the same places

      The client framed the portal as a trade-off between scholars and the public, but both groups hit the same walls. A round-one researcher asked for something like a card catalog, one card per object with every key fact. Another couldn't find how to request research access. In round two, a research-minded participant had to piece together an illustration's history from scattered fields. Plain-language records could likely serve both groups, though that still needs testing.

    06 · Recommendations

    Where the recommendations are heading

    We scored each round-one issue by severity, task importance and how many people hit it. Of 35 issues, missing on-view information ranked first (6 of 8 participants), then missing acquisition history (5 of 8) and hard-to-find collections (4 of 8). We're folding round two in now. Recommendations are forming around four ideas:

    • A summary at the top of every record: what it is, when it was made, how it got here, and whether you can see it
    • Collection Connections as a front door
    • Results that lead with images
    • One connected system instead of three separate catalogs

    07 · Reflection

    What I'd do differently

    I'd review the task script with the client before the first session, which would have saved a round. I'd test screen sharing a day ahead, since setup took fifteen minutes of one session. I'd get clean transcripts. And I'd log unspoken actions from day one.

    Thank you to our 12 participants, and to The Huntington's team for being candid about who the portal was built for.

    Case study · Web · team project

    NYPL Events redesign

    People could find New York Public Library events, but not always the confidence to go. Research into how they actually plan led to eight changes, from new filters to clearer RSVPs.

    Role
    UX research and design
    Team
    Team project
    Scope
    Homepage, event listings, filters and event pages
    Methods
    Card sorting, tree testing, interviews, usability tests
    6research methods
    3competitors compared
    8design changes

    01 · The problem

    Finding an event wasn't the hard part

    People could discover events on the NYPL site, but it didn't always give them the information or the confidence they needed to decide whether an event was relevant or worth attending.

    Along the way they ran into confusing filters, inconsistent navigation, information-heavy pages and unclear registration actions.

    02 · Research

    People plan around their own lives

    • People think about their own plans

      They looked for events by personal circumstance: what's on this weekend, what's nearby, what they could go to with friends. The site organized events by institutional categories.

    • Practical details decide

      Location, time, accessibility and registration requirements mattered most when deciding whether to attend.

    03 · Process

    Six ways of asking

    1. Card sorting

      How people group events in their heads.

    2. Tree testing

      Whether they could find things in the structure.

    3. User interviews

      How they decide what to go to.

    4. Paper prototype testing

      Early usability tests before any polish.

    5. Competitive analysis

      Meetup, Eventbrite and Brooklyn Public Library.

    6. Iterative prototyping

      Refining the design round by round.

    04 · Solution

    Built around plans, not categories

    • Reorganized homepage content to match users' mental models
    • Rebuilt filters around location, time, accessibility, topic and age group
    • Added time-of-day filters and map-based location selection
    • Supported multiple filters with clearer active filter states
    • Improved navigation with breadcrumbs and consistent sidebar behavior
    • Simplified event cards to highlight essential information
    • Made RSVP buttons more visible and consistent
    • Added calendar integration and related event recommendations

    05 · Reflection

    Confidence is part of usability

    Usability isn't always about whether someone can find something. Sometimes the bigger problem is whether they have enough information and confidence to act on what they've found.

    What this taught me

    It also taught me to translate research findings into specific design decisions, rather than changing things based on visual preference alone.

    Case study · Web · accessibility research

    Amon Carter Museum accessibility

    How do visitors with disabilities use the Amon Carter Museum of American Art's website to plan a visit? We evaluated what gets in their way before they ever arrive.

    Role
    Accessibility research
    Team
    Team project
    Scope
    Homepage and Plan Your Visit
    Focus
    WCAG evaluation, inclusive design, pre-visit information
    7research methods and checks
    2key insights
    5design implications

    01 · The problem

    Accessibility starts before the visit

    Accessibility isn't limited to physical accommodations inside a building. Visitors also need accessible, accurate and detailed information to know whether a museum can meet their needs.

    Planning can mean researching accessible entrances, transportation, seating, restrooms, sensory conditions, navigation and available accommodations. When that information is missing, vague or hard to find, visitors face more uncertainty and more planning work.

    02 · Research

    General statements aren't enough

    • Accessibility isn't one category

      Museums often present accessibility as a single broad topic, even though visitors have very different needs.

    • Broad statements leave people guessing

      General accessibility statements often don't give someone enough detail to know whether a specific space or experience will work for them.

    03 · Process

    Checking the site, then the information

    1. Desk research

      Accessibility barriers in museums.

    2. Museum review

      How museums communicate accessibility.

    3. WCAG spot checks

      Color use, non-text contrast, keyboard access, text resizing, motion and auto-updating content.

    4. Content review

      How clear and organized the pre-visit information is.

    04 · Design implications

    Specific, findable, independent

    • Make accessibility information specific, not generalized
    • Let visitors find relevant accommodations without digging through unrelated pages
    • Support independent decision-making
    • Integrate accessibility into the whole visitor experience, not a separate corner
    • Treat technical accessibility and accessible information as equally important

    05 · Reflection

    More than a checklist

    Accessibility isn't simply a checklist of technical requirements. It's also about whether people have the information and resources they need to participate.

    What this taught me

    I'm especially interested in how small information gaps can create big barriers for people with different abilities and needs.

    Case study · Mobile app · Pratt, fall 2026

    Pounce: An App to Unite Cat Lovers

    Designing Pounce, a community app for finding NYC's shop cats, and making sure the information is current enough to trust.

    Role
    UX designer and researcher. I researched the problems people face finding cats, ran two user interviews and one usability session, and helped synthesize findings.
    Team
    Elizabeth, Kat, Theresa and me
    Course
    Digital Product Design (INFO 646), Pratt Institute, fall 2026
    Methods
    Desk research, competitive and SWOT analysis, interviews, journey mapping, SCAMPER, MoSCoW, sketching, a mid-fidelity prototype and usability tests
    9interviews with people who live in or visit NYC
    7moderated usability tests
    47usability issues scored

    01 · The problem

    People already hunt for shop cats, with nothing reliable to use

    New York's bodega and shop cats have a real following. The @shopcatsshow account has over 777,000 followers, and ShopCats, an app for finding cats in businesses, passed 130,000 downloads before it shut down for financial reasons. Since then, people have crowdsourced the same information by hand. One 2026 Reddit post asking for Austin shop cats got over 1,500 upvotes, and another poster noted the cat maps they'd found were years out of date.

    The need outlived the app. What was missing was a way to know the information was still true.

    02 · Competitive analysis

    No competitor kept sightings current

    We compared social accounts, cat maps and gamified apps, then ran SWOT analyses on the two closest, Catmaps.nyc and Cat Collector. None combined reliable locations, detailed cat profiles and an active community. Cat Collector had few active users and no way to check whether a sighting was still valid.

    That pointed us at freshness and community upkeep, not just another map.

    03 · Research

    Looking past "cat lovers"

    Our first framing centered on people who love cats. Feedback pushed us to ask a harder question: why do people contribute to community platforms, and what keeps them contributing? We rewrote our interview script around online communities, trust and sharing, and interviewed 9 people who live in or regularly visit NYC.

    We coded every quote and grouped them into four themes:

    Interview themes, 9 participants
    ThemeParticipantsWhat it means for us
    Trust and credibility9 of 9Show how recent information is, and who backs it up
    Sharing and discovery8 of 9Put discovery and practical details in one place
    Community connections7 of 9People stay for the people, so build social ties
    Motivation to contribute7 of 9Make the first post easy, then reward continued posting

    If the last review was, like, 2 years ago… I would probably not visit there.

    Interview participant

    Recency came up again and again. Another participant checked information against friends: "Having a friend back it up usually is a good indicator." For Pounce, that meant a sighting without a timestamp would be worth little.

    04 · Defining the problem

    The real cost was a wasted trip

    Our journey map followed someone choosing a place to go. Their mood dropped at evaluation and bottomed out at verification, when they were bouncing between apps to check whether a place was even open.

    As an NYC resident who uses community recommendations to find things to do near me, I need accurate information about whether those places and activities are still available, so I can make plans without risking a wasted trip.

    Our problem statement, after several rewrites

    Our guiding question was how to help people feel reassured that community information is accurate.

    05 · Ideation

    We kept the ideas that answered trust

    We used SCAMPER to generate ideas and dot-voted on them. The strongest idea also protected the cats: show the nearest intersection instead of an exact address.

    Each of us then sketched a different direction: a random cat "adventure," an interactive map with cat profiles, and a Pokémon Go-style collecting game. We dot-voted on the strongest pieces and combined them into low-fidelity flows.

    We used MoSCoW to scope the first version. Finding a nearby cat, verifying reliability and browsing posts were must-haves. Gamification was a should-have, kept in a supporting role so it wouldn't distract from actually finding cats.

    06 · Usability testing

    Testing showed what earned trust, and what blocked people

    We ran 7 in-person, moderated think-aloud sessions on the mid-fidelity prototype at Pratt's Manhattan campus, November 10–16. Participants worked through six scenarios, from signing up to finding a nearby cat, deciding whether it was there right now, and sharing a visit. They rated each task from 1 (very easy) to 5 (very difficult).

    The trust signal worked. Every participant said the "Last seen" label made them believe the cat would be there, and deciding whether Prince was there now was the easiest task (average 1.1). Finding a nearby cat was the hardest (average 3.0).

    We scored 47 issues by impact, task importance and how many people hit them. Three stood out:

    • Stories set the wrong expectation

      Four of seven expected "Nearby Cats" in the home stories to help them find cats.

    • The add button looked like zoom

      Two mistook the paw "+" button on the map for zoom.

    • People worried about the cats

      Two worried about the cats' safety and owners getting in trouble. A trust app can't only be trusted by its users. Shop owners have to trust it too.

    07 · Redesign

    Then we redesigned what broke

    On the map, we added a locate button, labeled the add button, and added a "Cats near you" list with distances and last-seen times, so finding a cat no longer depends on reading the map.

    On the home screen, we renamed the story bubbles by place and theme, like Greenpoint and Bodega Cats, so it's clear what each one shows.

    We also added a safety screen before anyone shares a cat. It explains that businesses approve listings, asks people to protect privacy, and shows how to report a concern.

    08 · Reflection

    What I'd do differently

    I'd pin down the problem statement earlier. We rewrote it several times, and each version shifted what we researched. I'd also test the prototype's interactions before sessions. Map pins that didn't respond to taps made the hardest task harder, and that blurs whether the problem was the design or the prototype.
